    │       To recreate this image, follow these steps:
    │       
    │       * Start with a white background.
    │       * Use black text.
    │       * Divide the text into two sections with headings:
    │       	+ "On Power-Under"

    │       * In the "On Power-Under" section, describe the expression of powerless rage and its impact on others.

    │       The full text is as follows:
    │       
    │       On Power-Under:
    │       The expression of powerless rage is like the flailing of someone who is literally drowning. The survivor, who is enacting the moment of trauma, is caught up in a desperate struggle for psychic survival. Someone in such a state cannot possibly gauge the impact of their actions on others. And to someone who is feeling powerless, acted upon, and profoundly victimized, it is typically inconceivable that we could be posing any threat or danger to others. Yet the flailing of a drowning person poses a very real danger to anyone who approaches, and so can the expressed rage of a survivor in a traumatic state. The irony is that someone acting from an internal state of sheer powerlessness can have an enormously powerful impact on anyone in their path. This is the dynamic that I am calling power-under.
    │       
    │       On Nonviolence as Self-Protection:
    │       Nonviolent resistance is extraordinarily relevant to the situation of trauma survivors. In most cases the lasting, major damage caused by abuse is not physical but emotional and psychological - the crushing of human spirit. Efforts at self-protection by trauma survivors that demonize or dehumanize the Other unwittingly and tragically compound the damage to our own spirits. A central challenge faced by trauma survivors is how to resist malevolence and violation by valuing rather than diminishing human life.
    │       
    │       Nonviolence redefines the terms of self-protection. It poses an entirely new set of questions: How can I safeguard my human spirit? How can I try to defend and protect myself physically without compromising or crushing my own humanity? How can I resist acts of abuse and oppression without dehumanizing my oppressors? Or anyone else? How can I maintain

1280867457201291264 [2020-07-08] @mykola 💜 22 🔁 2 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
Interesting tweet + responses on renaming "toxic masculinity" to "traumatized masculinity".

My gut reaction was dismissive, but thinking about it I see some value here. The discourse right now lacks any way to bring traumatized men in from the cold. https://t.co/t9s1GodqIX
  [Quoting @Malcolm_Ocean: @QiaochuYuan This excerpt points at the problem of the term "toxic masculinity" and the need for a term like "traumatized masculinity": > "Efforts at self-protection by trauma survivors that demonize or dehumanize the Other unwittingly and tragically compound the damage to our own spirits." https://t.co/YPQYPSSc4k]
↓
1280867458392489989 [2020-07-08] @mykola 💜 11 🔁 2 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
Whether we focus on calling it toxic masculinity (focus on behavior) or traumatized masculinity (focus on internal motivations) we have to center the harm it can and does do, every day.

But part of me yearns for this more inclusive language, because most men need help not blame.
↓
1280868775206797313 [2020-07-08] @mykola 💜 5
And don't get me started on the overuse and frankly abuse of the term gaslighting, which is a real phenomenon but which doesn't describe every time someone disagrees about what happened.

I used to believe "accidental gaslighting" was a thing, but I no longer think so.
↓
1280868776196681728 [2020-07-08] @mykola 💜 10 🔁 1
I think maybe what I'm feeling is: terms like gaslighting and toxic masculinity, while addressing real phenomena that need to be addressed, do so in a way that discounts the potential presence of good faith on the part of the actor.

Sometimes we need exactly that. But not always
↓
1280869464431562754 [2020-07-08] @mykola 💜 7
"Myk, you just don't get it. These words are used because they center the victims."

So like, I DO get it, and I understand the logic behind it. 

Hi, I'm one of the men who has largely been able to work through what felt like a hostile onboarding process for being a Good Man.
↓
1280869465404702720 [2020-07-08] @mykola 💜 12 🔁 1
I kinda feel like maybe if we provided a paved road to that destination and didn't require quite so much self-negation we might find that a lot more men are willing to meet us here.

Should we HAVE to center them? I dunno. Is that the right question? What outcomes do we want?

New model: masc/femme is not a spectrum, but rather two unrelated groups of traits. It's possible to be high or low in both. More of both is generally desirable, regardless of gender. "Toxic masculinity" is nonsensical. "Toxic non-femininity" is a better framing. Thoughts?
↓

Open to feedback https://t.co/7ih7V7uH9U
  [Quoting @xsphi: @typicalTyper Masculinity: strength (physical, mental, social), proactive decision making, emotional resilience, applied rationality  Femininity: empathy, kindness, intuitive understanding of complex systems, an eye for aesthetics  Both possibly correlated with but not dependent on gender]
↓
1341520047626326016 [2020-12-22] @xsphi 💜 1
The most useful part of this perspective to me is that I can stop thinking in terms of tradeoffs. I don't have to sacrifice anything except time and effort to gain more of the traits that I want.

1498475099673952263 [2022-03-01] @vividvoid 💜 335 🔁 31
It's technically true that patriarchy is responsible for the male mental health crisis, and many of men's struggles with emotional vulnerability. 

But to put it this way is itself benevolent sexism: it hides the deep emotional and psychological damage done by female aggression.
↓
1498475100869312516 [2022-03-01] @vividvoid 💜 134 🔁 4
When women get aggressive, it tends to be social and symbolic, not physical. That is, they tend to attack relationships, rather than bodies - they sabotage bonds, smear reputations, and attempt to damage others' egos - self-relationships - via emotional wounding.
↓
1498475102068883456 [2022-03-01] @vividvoid 💜 86 🔁 2
Men are not uniquely victims of this, ofc, women can be especially vicious with one another, as any woman can attest. Intrasexual competition is real, and in many ways, women have unique vulnerabilities to emotional and relational damage, as their power is so linked to the social
↓
1498475103264272384 [2022-03-01] @vividvoid 💜 90 🔁 3
But since the time of the MeToo movement, men have also become much more vulnerable to women's aggression. An accusation carries far more weight. A woman's tears, her emotional distress, shuts down debate and greatly limits men's social options - and ability to defend themselves.
↓
1498475104522489859 [2022-03-01] @vividvoid 💜 116 🔁 2
The presumption of male-as-aggressor and female-as-victim remains culturally unassailable, despite the new asymmetries. So many men - including me, and many I know - have been deeply damaged by female aggression, with absolutely no prospect for justice or recourse.
↓
1498475105692766213 [2022-03-01] @vividvoid 💜 142 🔁 5
If our discourse were ecological, we would recognize men are inseparable from the women in their lives. We'd talk less about "toxic masculinity" and a lot more about traumas that alienate men from the natural authenticity and vulnerability that is their birthright as human beings
↓
1498682119245209602 [2022-03-01] @CountJ0ecool 💜 1 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
@VividVoid_ part of what makes the noun-phrase "toxic masculinity" so toxic is that it shames men for appearing emotionally vulnerable, which in turn makes them MORE vulnerable by isolating them from needed support

that the term is misleading is itself a kind of fem-coded violence imo
